newsitem.title: UK: UK construction industry to grow in 1997/98 - survey.
newsitem.headline: UK construction industry to grow in 1997/98 - survey.

text.p: The UK construction industry is finally set to emerge from its six-year recession, with a small rise in 1996 output and continued growth until the end of 1998, the Building Materials Producers group said on Monday.
Total output for 1996 is expected to be up 0.5 percent, with 2.5 percent growth seen in 1997 and 1998.
But the BMP's latest industry forecast warned that growth
would continue to lag behind the levels enjoyed by the rest of the UK economy. The building industry's lagging performance was blamed on under-investment in the public sector due to governments cuts.
Most of the increase in business stems from the private sector taking off, with a healthier private housing market and more spending on commercial property.

The private housing market recovery is seen spreading to other regions from the South East of England. New starts are expected to reach 160,000 by 1998, the survey found. Repair and maintenance on properties in this sector is also expected to rise by five percent.
"Commmercial entertainment" orders are seen growing up to 1998, fuelled by projects to celebrate the Millennium. Private sector growth is seen off-setting a downbeat public sector.
Total public sector investment, in contrast, is seen falling by seven percent by the close of 1996, by five percent in 1997 and two percent in 1998.
Recent UK Budget cuts in the Housing Corporation's funding is expected to result in public housing starts of 24,000 in 1997 and 20,000 in 1998, with reduced spending on maintenance.

Delays to private finance projects -- the government policy to fund public infrastructure through private funding -- is seen delaying projects in school and health, resulting in a nine percent fall in non-housing public output in 1996.

"The outlook is better, better than it has been for some time. We've had a pretty torrid few years, with construction output falling 10 percent," Robert Napier, chief executive of building materials group Redland and president of the National Council of Building Material Producers, said.
He told a briefing builders understood the government's need to "balance the books" and did not want a "splurge in spending".

"But we are saying to the government in the run-up to an election (due by May 1997) that on the day of reckoning Joe Public will say, "Why was nothing done about the state of schools, hospitals, roads?'"
